code.title: Orientation test with the cross product (no slopes, no division)
code.python:
# Cross product of AB and AC. Only multiply and subtract, so it is exact.
def cross(ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy):
    return (bx - ax) * (cy - ay) - (by - ay) * (cx - ax)


def main():
    # Each row is A, B, C as ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy.
    tests = [(0, 0, 4, 0, 2, 3), (0, 0, 4, 0, 2, -3), (0, 0, 2, 2, 5, 5), (1, 1, 1, 5, 0, 3)]
    for t in tests:
        c = cross(*t)
        # Positive = left turn, negative = right turn, zero = collinear.
        turn = "left turn" if c > 0 else ("right turn" if c < 0 else "collinear")
        print(f"A({t[0]},{t[1]}) B({t[2]},{t[3]}) C({t[4]},{t[5]}): cross = {c} -> {turn}")
    # The last test has a vertical line A->B: a slope would divide by zero.
    # Time O(1) per test, space O(1).


main()

followUps:
Coordinates up to about 109 in absolute value are safe; beyond that the cross product can overflow a 64-bit integer.

If every coordinate is at most C in size, a difference such as B.x − A.x can reach 2C, each product can reach 4C2, and the subtraction of two products can reach 8C2. A signed 64-bit integer holds up to about 9.22 × 1018, so 8C2 ≤ 9.22 × 1018 gives C ≤ about 1.07 × 109. With C = 109 the worst value is 8 × 1018, which just fits.

For larger inputs use a 128-bit type (__int128 in C++), BigInteger, or Python integers. In Java, Math.multiplyExact throws instead of silently wrapping around.

Turn them into integers first: multiply latitude and longitude by a fixed scale, round, and then use the same exact integer cross product.

A scale of 106 keeps about 11 cm of detail. Longitude 180° becomes 180,000,000, far below the 109 overflow limit. A scale of 107 (about 1 cm) gives 1.8 × 109, which is too big for 64-bit products, so subtract a local origin first or use 128-bit maths.

If you must stay in doubles, never test cross == 0. Compare against a tolerance that grows with the input, for example |cross| ≤ 1e-12 · |AB| · |AC|, and use that one function everywhere.

Also remember that latitude and longitude are angles on a sphere. For fences larger than a city, project the points to a flat map before doing plane geometry.

Split the points into the upper and lower half of the plane, then order points inside the same half with the cross product.

  1. Give each point a half: 0 if y > 0, or y == 0 and x > 0; otherwise 1.
  2. A point in half 0 comes before a point in half 1.
  3. Inside one half, a comes before b when cross(a, b) > 0, meaning b is counter-clockwise from a.
int half(P p) { return (p.y > 0 || (p.y == 0 && p.x > 0)) ? 0 : 1; }
boolean less(P a, P b) {
  if (half(a) != half(b)) return half(a) < half(b);
  return a.x * b.y - a.y * b.x > 0;
}

Example: (1,0), (0,1), (−1,0), (0,−1) sort in exactly that order. The halves are needed because the cross product alone cannot order points more than 180° apart. Sorting costs O(N log N) and stays exact, with no atan2 rounding.

code.title: Segment intersection with four orientation tests and the collinear cases

followUps:
Use a sweep line (the Shamos–Hoey algorithm): move a vertical line from left to right and only compare segments that are neighbours on that line.

  1. Sort the 2N end points by x.
  2. Keep the segments that currently cross the sweep line in a balanced tree, ordered by their y at the line.
  3. At a left end point, insert the segment and test it against the one just above and the one just below.
  4. At a right end point, remove the segment and test its two former neighbours against each other.
  5. Stop at the first hit.

This works because two segments that cross must become neighbours in the tree just before their crossing point. Each of the 2N events costs O(log N), so the total is O(N log N) time and O(N) space, compared with O(N2) for testing every pair. Listing all K crossings needs Bentley–Ottmann, O((N + K) log N).

Keep the answer as two fractions with the same whole-number denominator, and divide only if someone needs a decimal.

With r = P2 − P1, s = Q2 − Q1, d = r × s and n = (Q1 − P1) × s, the point is P1 + (n/d)·r:

long d = cross(r, s);                 // 0 means parallel
long n = cross(sub(q1, p1), s);
long xNum = p1.x * d + n * r.x;       // x = xNum / d
long yNum = p1.y * d + n * r.y;       // y = yNum / d
// divide each pair by its gcd, keep d positive

Example: (0,0)–(4,4) and (0,4)–(4,0). r = (4,4), s = (4,−4), d = 4·(−4) − 4·4 = −32, n = 0·(−4) − 4·4 = −16. Then xNum = −64 and yNum = −64, so the point is (−64/−32, −64/−32) = (2, 2).

The numerators multiply three coordinates together, so use 128-bit or big integers once coordinates pass about 106. Time and space are O(1).

code.title: Andrew's monotone chain convex hull

followUps:
Because a convex hull algorithm can be used to sort numbers, and sorting by comparisons cannot be done faster than N log N.

Take the numbers 3, 1, 2. Turn each x into the point (x, x2): (3,9), (1,1), (2,4). These lie on a parabola, which curves one way, so every point is a hull corner. Walking the hull counter-clockwise from the leftmost point gives (1,1), (2,4), (3,9), which is the sorted order 1, 2, 3.

Building the points and reading the hull take O(N). So if some algorithm found hulls in less than N log N time, you could sort in less than N log N time, which is known to be impossible in the comparison (algebraic decision tree) model. The bound only loosens when the hull has few corners; then O(N log H) is possible.

Run rotating calipers over the hull: the two farthest points are always hull corners, and one walk around the hull finds them.

  1. Build the hull in counter-clockwise order, H corners.
  2. For each edge i → i+1, move a second pointer j forward while the triangle (i, i+1, j+1) has a larger area than (i, i+1, j). Area is the cross product, so no square roots.
  3. Compare the squared distances from i and from i+1 to j with the best so far.

The pointer j never moves backwards, so the walk is O(H). With the hull the total is O(N log N) time and O(N) space, instead of O(N2) for all pairs.

Example: for the square (0,0), (4,0), (4,4), (0,4) the answer is a diagonal with squared distance 42 + 42 = 32. Keep distances squared and in 64-bit integers so the result is exact.

Graham scan sorts by angle around a pivot, and all its traps come from points that have the same angle. Monotone chain sorts by (x, y) only, so it has none of them.

  • Same angle from the pivot: ties must be broken by distance, nearest first. Example: pivot (0,0) with (1,1) and (2,2). If (2,2) comes first, (1,1) is pushed later and can wrongly stay on the hull.
  • The last ray: if you want to keep collinear border points, the final group of equal-angle points must be reversed (farthest first), or the points on the closing edge are lost.
  • Pivot choice: lowest y, and lowest x among those. Copies of the pivot must be removed.
  • atan2: floating-point angles make equal angles look different. Compare with the cross product instead.

Both algorithms cost O(N log N); monotone chain is simply harder to get wrong.

code.title: Jarvis march (gift wrapping): O(N*H), fast when the hull is tiny
code.python:
def cross(a, b, c):
    return (b[0] - a[0]) * (c[1] - a[1]) - (b[1] - a[1]) * (c[0] - a[0])


pts = [(2, 2), (5, 1), (0, 0), (6, 5), (1, 6), (3, 3), (4, 2), (2, 4)]
n = len(pts)
print("Points:" + "".join(f" ({x},{y})" for x, y in pts))
# Start from the leftmost point: it is certainly on the hull.
start = 0
for i in range(1, n):
    if pts[i][0] < pts[start][0]:
        start = i
hull = []
cur, tests = start, 0
while True:
    hull.append(pts[cur])
    # Find the point with every other point on its left: one O(N) scan.
    cand = (cur + 1) % n
    for q in range(n):
        tests += 1
        if cross(pts[cur], pts[cand], pts[q]) < 0:
            cand = q  # q is to the right, so it wraps tighter
    cur = cand
    if cur == start:  # stop when the wrap closes
        break
print("Hull:" + "".join(f" ({x},{y})" for x, y in hull))
print(f"N = {n}, H = {len(hull)}, orientation tests = N*H = {tests}")
# Time O(N*H), space O(1) besides the output. No sorting is needed.

followUps:
Chan's algorithm guesses the hull size m as 4, 16, 256, 65536, …, squaring the guess each time it turns out too small. That is m = 22t for t = 1, 2, 3, …

One round with guess m: split the points into N/m groups of m, build each group's hull (O(N log m) in total), then take at most m gift-wrapping steps, where each step finds the best next point of every group hull by binary search (O((N/m) log m) per step). If the hull has not closed after m steps, H is larger than m: stop and square m.

A round costs O(N log m) = O(N · 2t). The costs double each round, so the sum is about twice the last round, and the last round has log m below 2 log H. Total: O(N log H).

Example: H = 100 fails with 4 and 16 and succeeds with 256: N·(2 + 4 + 8) = 14N steps. Merely doubling m would need log H rounds and cost O(N log2 H).

QuickHull and randomized incremental algorithms generalise best; they are what real 3D libraries use (Qhull, which SciPy and MATLAB call, is QuickHull).

The 2D favourites do not carry over. Graham scan and monotone chain depend on putting points in one sorted order (by angle or by x), and points in space have no such order around a hull made of faces. Gift wrapping does extend, but costs O(N × faces). Divide and conquer reaches O(N log N) in 3D, but its merge step is hard to code.

QuickHull in 3D: start with a tetrahedron of 4 extreme points, give each outside point to a face that can see it, take the farthest point of some face, remove all faces that point can see, and connect the point to the rim (the horizon) of the hole with new triangles. Points inside are thrown away early. Typical cost is O(N log N); the worst case is O(N2).

code.title: Shoelace formula: right for ordered simple polygons, wrong for a bow-tie
code.python:
# Returns twice the signed area: positive for counter-clockwise order.
def twice_area(xs, ys):
    total = 0
    n = len(xs)
    for i in range(n):
        j = (i + 1) % n  # wrap around to the first vertex
        total += xs[i] * ys[j] - xs[j] * ys[i]
    return total


def report(name, xs, ys):
    pts = "".join(f" ({x},{y})" for x, y in zip(xs, ys))
    t = twice_area(xs, ys)
    # Keep 2*area as an integer; divide only when printing.
    print(f"{name}:{pts} -> signed 2*area = {t}, area = {abs(t) // 2}")


report("Rectangle, counter-clockwise", [0, 4, 4, 0], [0, 0, 3, 3])
report("Rectangle, clockwise", [0, 0, 4, 4], [0, 3, 3, 0])
# Same four corners in a crossing order: the two lobes cancel out.
report("Bow-tie (self-intersecting)", [0, 4, 4, 0], [0, 3, 0, 3])
# Time O(N), space O(1).

followUps:
Use Pick's theorem: for a simple polygon whose corners have whole-number coordinates, Area = I + B/2 − 1, so I = Area − B/2 + 1, where I counts inside grid points and B counts grid points on the border.

  1. Get 2·Area from the shoelace sum.
  2. B is the sum of gcd(|dx|, |dy|) over all edges.
  3. I = (2·Area − B + 2) / 2.
long twice = 0, b = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  int j = (i + 1) % n;
  twice += x[i] * y[j] - x[j] * y[i];
  b += gcd(Math.abs(x[j] - x[i]), Math.abs(y[j] - y[i]));
}
long inside = (Math.abs(twice) - b + 2) / 2;

Example: rectangle (0,0), (4,0), (4,3), (0,3). 2·Area = 24, B = 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14, I = (24 − 14 + 2)/2 = 6. Check: x from 1 to 3 and y from 1 to 2 is 3 × 2 = 6 points. Time O(N log C) for the gcds, space O(1).

Reuse the shoelace terms: the centroid is the area-weighted average of the centroids of the triangles (origin, Pi, Pi+1). It is not the average of the corners.

With ci = xi·yi+1 − xi+1·yi and signed area A = ½·Σci:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  int j = (i + 1) % n;
  double c = x[i] * y[j] - x[j] * y[i];
  a2 += c; sx += (x[i] + x[j]) * c; sy += (y[i] + y[j]) * c;
}
double cx = sx / (3 * a2), cy = sy / (3 * a2);

Example: rectangle (0,0), (4,0), (4,3), (0,3). The c values are 0, 12, 12, 0, so a2 = 24. sx = 8·12 + 4·12 = 144 and sy = 3·12 + 6·12 = 108. Centroid = (144/72, 108/72) = (2, 1.5), the middle of the rectangle.

Time O(N), space O(1). Keep the signed area (no absolute value) so clockwise input still works, and guard against area 0.

code.title: Point in polygon by ray casting, with the vertex and boundary cases
code.python:
PX = [0, 6, 6, 3, 0]
PY = [0, 0, 6, 3, 6]  # a square with a notch cut in the top


def cross(ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy):
    return (bx - ax) * (cy - ay) - (by - ay) * (cx - ax)


def locate(x, y):
    n = len(PX)
    crossings = 0
    for i in range(n):
        j = (i + 1) % n
        ax, ay, bx, by = PX[i], PY[i], PX[j], PY[j]
        # On the edge itself: collinear and inside the edge's bounding box.
        if (cross(ax, ay, bx, by, x, y) == 0 and min(ax, bx) <= x <= max(ax, bx)
                and min(ay, by) <= y <= max(ay, by)):
            return "on the boundary"
        if ay > by:  # make A the lower end
            ax, ay, bx, by = bx, by, ax, ay
        # Half-open rule: count the edge only if low.y <= y < high.y (skips horizontal edges).
        # The ray to the right crosses it when the point is left of the upward edge.
        if ay <= y < by and cross(ax, ay, bx, by, x, y) > 0:
            crossings += 1
    return "inside" if crossings % 2 == 1 else "outside"  # odd number of crossings = inside


print("Polygon: (0,0) (6,0) (6,6) (3,3) (0,6)")
for x, y in [(1, 1), (3, 4), (1, 3), (7, 3), (6, 2), (3, 3)]:
    print(f"Point ({x},{y}): {locate(x, y)}")
# Point (1,3) is the tricky one: its ray passes exactly through the vertex (3,3).
# Time O(N) per query, space O(1).

followUps:
Do not test a point against every fence. Build an index that turns a point into a short list of candidate fences, and run the exact test only on those.

  • Index: cover each fence with grid cells (S2 cells or geohashes) and store a map from cell to fence ids. Mark cells that lie fully inside a fence, so a hit there needs no polygon test at all.
  • Query: compute the point's cell in O(1), look it up, and run ray casting only for the few fences whose border passes through that cell.
  • Serving: the index is read-mostly, so keep it in memory as an unchanging snapshot, copy it to several servers and split it by region. Build updates in the background and swap the snapshot in one step.

A lookup plus one or two exact tests takes a few microseconds, so one core handles roughly 105 queries per second and a few replicas give headroom.

They differ only when the polygon crosses itself or its loops overlap; for a simple polygon both always give the same answer.

Even-odd counts how many edges a ray crosses and says "inside" when the count is odd. The winding number counts how many times the border goes around the point: +1 for each edge crossing the ray upwards, −1 for each crossing downwards, and "inside" means the total is not zero.

Example: a five-pointed star drawn with one stroke. A ray from the small pentagon in the middle crosses 2 edges, so even-odd says outside. But the stroke goes around the middle twice, so the winding number is 2 and the non-zero rule says inside.

Both cost O(N) per query. Use the winding number for traced paths (a GPS track that overlaps itself). Use even-odd when overlapping rings are meant to cut holes.

code.title: Reservoir sampling (k = 2): every item is kept equally often
code.python:
seed = 42


# Small fixed random generator so every language prints the same numbers.
def rnd():
    global seed
    seed = seed * 48271 % 2147483647
    return seed


n, k, trials = 6, 2, 30000
kept = [0] * (n + 1)
for _ in range(trials):
    res = [0] * k
    for i in range(n):  # the stream is the items 1..6, index i = 0..5
        item = i + 1
        if i < k:
            res[i] = item  # the first k items fill the reservoir
        else:
            j = rnd() % (i + 1)  # j is uniform in [0, i], i included
            if j < k:
                res[j] = item  # happens with probability k/(i+1)
    for x in res:
        kept[x] += 1
print(f"Stream 1..6, sample size 2, {trials} runs. Expected about {trials * k // n} each.")
for item in range(1, n + 1):
    print(f"item {item} kept {kept[item]} times")
# Time O(N) per pass over the stream, space O(k).

followUps:
Algorithm L does not flip a coin for every item. It works out, with one random draw, how many items to skip before the next replacement, and jumps straight there.

  1. Fill the reservoir with the first k items. Set W = exp(ln(rand()) / k).
  2. Skip floor(ln(rand()) / ln(1 − W)) items.
  3. Put the next item into a random reservoir slot, then shrink W: W *= exp(ln(rand()) / k). Repeat from step 2.
i += (long) Math.floor(Math.log(rnd()) / Math.log(1 - W)) + 1;
if (i < n) {
  res[randInt(k)] = stream[i];
  W *= Math.exp(Math.log(rnd()) / k);
}

The skips get longer as the stream grows, because later items are rarely accepted. Random draws drop from N to about 3·k·ln(N/k). With k = 10 and N = 109 that is about 550 draws instead of a billion. The sample is still exactly uniform; memory stays O(k).

The newest item gets in too often, so the sample leans towards the end of the stream and is no longer uniform.

The item at index i must be accepted with probability k/(i+1), because it is one of i+1 items seen so far. Drawing j from [0, i − 1] has only i possible values, so the item is accepted with probability k/i, which is too high.

The damage is easiest to see with k = 1. At index 1, j is drawn from [0, 0], so j = 0 every time and the new item always replaces the old one. For the stream A, B, C the correct code returns each letter 1/3 of the time. The buggy code never returns A: B always replaces it, and then C replaces B half of the time, giving A 0, B 1/2, C 1/2. With general k, the item at index k is always accepted instead of with probability k/(k+1).

Tests on tiny streams with counted results catch this off-by-one quickly.

code.title: Weighted sampling with A-Res keys: per-server top-k merges into the global top-k
code.python:
seed = 42
key = [0.0] * 8


# Small fixed random generator so every language prints the same numbers.
def rnd01():
    global seed
    seed = seed * 48271 % 2147483647
    return seed / 2147483647.0


# Keep the k ids with the largest keys (a min-heap of size k does this on a real stream).
def top_k(ids, k):
    return sorted(ids, key=lambda i: -key[i])[:k]


weight = [1, 1, 2, 1, 8, 1, 1, 6]
k = 3
print(f"Weights of items 0..7: {weight}, sample size {k}")
# A-Res: key = u^(1/weight). A heavy item gets a key close to 1.
for i in range(8):
    key[i] = rnd01() ** (1.0 / weight[i])
a = top_k([0, 1, 2, 3], k)  # server A saw items 0..3
b = top_k([4, 5, 6, 7], k)  # server B saw items 4..7
merged = top_k(a + b, k)    # merge = top-k of the two local top-k lists
glob = top_k(list(range(8)), k)
print(f"Server A keeps {a}, server B keeps {b}")
print(f"Merged sample {merged}, one-machine sample {glob}")
print("Same result: " + ("yes" if merged == glob else "no"))
# Time O(N log k) with heaps (this demo sorts), space O(k) per server.

followUps:
An A-Res key belongs to the item alone, so it means the same thing on every server. A plain reservoir slot only has meaning together with how many events that server saw.

With keys, the global sample is "the k largest keys anywhere". Any item in the global top k is also in its own server's top k, so the union of the local top-k lists always contains the answer; one more top-k finishes the job.

With Algorithm R, a surviving item stands for a share of its stream. Example with k = 2: server A saw 10 events and server B saw 1000. Each item A kept stands for 5 events; each item B kept stands for 500. Mixing the four survivors evenly would give A half of the sample, although it produced under 1% of the events. So the merge needs the counts 10 and 1000 to pick from B about 99% of the time.

Give newer events a larger weight and reuse the weighted sampler: with weight w = eλt for an event at time t, old events fade out smoothly.

Computing eλt directly overflows, so work with logarithms. The A-Res key u1/w gives the same ranking as this score:

double e = -Math.log(rnd());            // rnd() in (0, 1)
double score = lambda * t - Math.log(e); // keep the k largest scores

Choose λ from a half-life h: λ = ln 2 / h. With a half-life of one hour, an event that is one hour older has half the weight, and one that is ten hours older has about 1/1000 of it.

Cost is the same as before: O(log k) per event with a min-heap, O(k) memory, and the scores still merge across servers. If you want a hard cut-off instead (only the last 24 hours), store time stamps and drop expired items from the heap.

code.title: Fisher-Yates vs the "obvious" shuffle: count every possible run for n = 3

followUps:
Give every record a random key and sort the file by that key with an external (on-disk) merge sort; the sorted order is a fair shuffle.

A cheaper two-pass version avoids the sort:

  1. Read the file once and append each record to one of M temporary files chosen at random.
  2. Load each temporary file into memory, shuffle it with Fisher–Yates, and append it to the output.

Example: 100 GB of data and 4 GB of memory. Use M = 64 files of about 1.6 GB each, so each one fits in memory. Every record is read and written twice, which is O(N) sequential disk work, against O(N log N) for the sort.

It is fair because a record's file is chosen independently and each file is then shuffled fairly. With random keys, use 64-bit keys so ties are practically impossible. If the result must be repeatable, save the seed.

Use it when you need one single loop through all the items, so that nobody ends up in their own place.

Sattolo's algorithm (pick j from [0, i − 1]) produces only permutations that form one cycle of length n, each with probability 1/(n − 1)!. For A, B, C it can only give BCA or CAB.

  • Secret Santa as one chain: everyone gives to exactly one other person, never to themselves, and following the gifts visits everybody.
  • Memory benchmarks: fill an array so that next[i] forms one random cycle; chasing the pointers then touches every cell once before repeating, which measures cache-miss latency.
  • Random round-robin order, such as a token passed around a ring.

It is not a uniform choice among all arrangements with no item in place: 4 people in two swapped pairs can never appear. Cost is O(N) time and O(1) extra space, the same as Fisher–Yates.

code.title: Randomized quickselect with a 3-way partition

followUps:
The recurrence is T(N) = T(N/5) + T(7N/10) + cN, and it solves to O(N) because 1/5 + 7/10 is less than 1.

  • cN: split into groups of 5, find each group's median, and partition around the pivot.
  • T(N/5): find the median of the N/5 group medians by a recursive call; that is the pivot.
  • T(7N/10): half of the groups have a median at or below the pivot, and each such group gives 3 elements at or below it. That is 3 · N/10 elements, so at most 7N/10 can be on the larger side (and the same the other way round).

Example: N = 100 gives 20 medians; the pivot beats at least 30 elements, so at most 70 remain.

The work per level shrinks by a factor of 9/10: cN·(1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + …) = 10cN. With groups of 3 the fractions are 1/3 + 2/3 = 1, nothing shrinks, and the result is O(N log N).

If the pivot is chosen by a fixed rule, anyone who knows the rule can build an input where every pivot is nearly the smallest or largest value, forcing N2 work.

Simplest case: "use the first element" on an already sorted array. Each round removes just one element, so the rounds cost N + (N − 1) + … ≈ N2/2 comparisons. For N = 106 that is 5 × 1011 instead of a few million.

Smarter fixed rules (middle element, median of three) only make the bad input harder to guess. McIlroy's "antiquicksort" builds it automatically: it answers the algorithm's comparisons lazily and fixes the values afterwards, so the pivots always turn out bad. A service that sorts or selects user-supplied data can be slowed to a halt this way.

Defences: pick pivots at random from a seed the attacker cannot see, or cap the depth and switch to median-of-medians or a heap (introselect).

code.title: Dynamic array growth: doubling is O(1) amortized, adding a fixed amount is not
code.python:
# Counts element copies made by n pushes. factor > 0 multiplies the capacity, otherwise step is added.
def copies(n, factor, step):
    capacity = 1 if factor > 0 else step
    size = 0
    copied = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        if size == capacity:
            copied += size  # a full array moves every element to the new block
            capacity = capacity * factor if factor > 0 else capacity + step
        size += 1
    return copied


for n in (1000, 100000):
    dbl = copies(n, 2, 0)
    add = copies(n, 0, 10)
    print(f"N = {n} pushes")
    # Total cost = N writes + copies. Doubling: copies are 1 + 2 + 4 + ... < 2N.
    print(f"  doubling:  copies = {dbl}, total = {n + dbl}, per push = {(n + dbl) // n} (rounded down)")
    # Adding 10 slots each time: copies are 10 + 20 + 30 + ... which grows like N*N/20.
    print(f"  add 10:    copies = {add}, total = {n + add}, per push = {(n + add) // n} (rounded down)")
# Doubling: O(1) amortized per push. Fixed step: O(N) amortized per push. Space O(N).

followUps:
Mainly to let the memory allocator reuse the blocks the array has already given back, and to waste less empty space.

With 2×, sizes go 16, 32, 64, 128. The blocks freed so far (16 + 32 = 48) are always smaller than the next request (128), so the array keeps climbing to fresh memory. With 1.5×, sizes go 16, 24, 36, 54, 81, 121. When 121 is needed, the freed blocks add up to 16 + 24 + 36 + 54 = 130, so the new block can fit in the old space. This works for any factor below about 1.618.

Slack is also smaller: just after growing, a 1.5× array is at most one third empty, a 2× array one half.

The price is more copying. The total number of copies is about N/(g − 1) for factor g: about N for 2×, about 2N for 1.5×. Both are O(1) amortized per push.

Use Φ = the number of 1 bits in the counter. With it, every increment has amortized cost exactly 2.

An increment turns t trailing 1s into 0s and then one 0 into a 1. Real cost: t + 1 bit flips. Change in Φ: −t + 1. Amortized cost = (t + 1) + (1 − t) = 2, whatever t is.

Example: 0111 → 1000 flips 4 bits. Φ falls from 3 to 1, a change of −2, so the amortized cost is 4 − 2 = 2. The cheap increments before it (each raising Φ) had already saved up for this expensive one.

Φ starts at 0 for a zero counter and can never be negative, so the real total is at most the amortized total: N increments flip at most 2N bits. That is O(1) amortized per increment, although one increment can flip log N bits.

code.title: De-amortizing a growing array: the worst single push, all-at-once vs incremental copy
code.python:
def main():
    n = 100000
    print(f"N = {n} pushes into a doubling array")

    # Version 1: when full, copy everything in one go (amortized O(1), but spiky).
    cap, size, total, worst = 1, 0, 0, 0
    for _ in range(n):
        cost = 1
        if size == cap:
            cost += size
            cap *= 2
        size += 1
        total += cost
        worst = max(worst, cost)
    print(f"Copy all at once: total work = {total}, worst single push = {worst}")

    # Version 2: when full, allocate the bigger block but move only 2 old elements per push.
    cap, size, total, worst = 1, 0, 0, 0
    to_move = 0  # old elements still waiting in the old block
    for _ in range(n):
        cost = 1
        moved = min(2, to_move)  # a small, fixed slice of the migration
        to_move -= moved
        cost += moved
        if size == cap:  # start a new migration, copy nothing yet
            to_move = size
            cap *= 2
        size += 1
        total += cost
        worst = max(worst, cost)
    print(f"Incremental copy: total work = {total}, worst single push = {worst}")
    # Same O(N) total, but the worst case per push drops from O(N) to O(1).
    # Price: two blocks are alive during a migration, so more memory.


main()

followUps:
While a migration is running, a lookup simply checks both tables: the old one first, then the new one.

The rules that keep this correct:

  • A key lives in exactly one table at any moment.
  • New keys are inserted only into the new table, so the old table never grows.
  • Updates and deletes look in both tables.
  • Every operation also moves one bucket (or a few) from the old table to the new one. When the old table is empty it is freed and the new table becomes the only one.

Example: growing from 8 to 16 buckets. Key 13 sat in old bucket 13 mod 8 = 5. If bucket 5 has not been moved yet, the lookup finds it in the old table; afterwards it is in new bucket 13 mod 16 = 13.

The cost is at most two bucket probes per lookup, and only during a migration. Each operation does O(1) extra work, so there is no long pause. Redis works this way.

They can stop holding, because an amortized bound assumes time only moves forward: each expensive step is paid for by the cheap steps before it, and it happens once.

With undo, a caller can go back to the state just before the expensive step and trigger it again and again. Example: a doubling array with 1024 elements and capacity 1024. Push copies 1024 elements; undo restores the old state; push copies 1024 again. Every push now costs O(N), not O(1). The same trick replays an expensive find in a union-find with path compression, or a deep access in a splay tree.

Fixes:

  • Use a structure with a worst-case bound per operation, such as union by rank without compression (O(log N) find, O(1) undo).
  • Make undo keep the paid-for work: keep the bigger capacity after the undo.
  • Use a persistent (versioned) structure designed for it.

code.title: A small skip list: coin-flip levels, insert by splicing pointers, top-down search
code.python:
MAXL = 4
key = [0]             # node 0 is the head
nxt = [[-1] * MAXL]   # nxt[node][level]; -1 means "none"
seed = 42


def rnd():  # small fixed generator so every language prints the same list
    global seed
    seed = seed * 48271 % 2147483647
    return seed


# Walk right while the next key is smaller, then drop one level.
def find_before(k):
    update = [0] * MAXL
    x = 0
    for l in range(MAXL - 1, -1, -1):
        while nxt[x][l] != -1 and key[nxt[x][l]] < k:
            x = nxt[x][l]
        update[l] = x  # last node before k on this level
    return update


def insert(k):
    update = find_before(k)
    lvl = 1
    while lvl < MAXL and rnd() % 2 == 0:  # coin flips decide the tower height
        lvl += 1
    key.append(k)
    nxt.append([-1] * MAXL)
    node = len(key) - 1
    for l in range(lvl):  # splice into each level: no rotations needed
        nxt[node][l] = nxt[update[l]][l]
        nxt[update[l]][l] = node


def contains(k):
    c = nxt[find_before(k)[0]][0]
    return c != -1 and key[c] == k


keys = [30, 10, 50, 20, 40, 60, 25]
print(f"Insert order: {keys}")
for k in keys:
    insert(k)
for l in range(MAXL - 1, -1, -1):
    line = f"Level {l}:"
    x = nxt[0][l]
    while x != -1:
        line += f" {key[x]}"
        x = nxt[x][l]
    print(line)
for k in (40, 35):
    print(f"search {k}: " + ("found" if contains(k) else "not found"))
# Expected O(log N) per search and insert, O(N) expected space.

followUps:
Each forward pointer also stores its span: how many bottom-level nodes it jumps over. Adding up the spans along the search path gives the element's position.

Rank of a key: search from the top level as usual and add the span of every pointer you follow. The total when you arrive is the rank. Example: the bottom level is 10, 20, 30, 40. On level 1 the head points to 20 with span 2, and 20 points to 40 with span 2. Searching for 40 follows both: 2 + 2 = 4, so 40 has rank 4 after two hops instead of four.

Element at rank r: move right while (total so far + span) ≤ r, otherwise go down a level.

Both are O(log N) expected. Insert and delete must fix the spans on the path: pointers above the new node's height get span + 1, and the pointers that are split share the old span. Redis uses this for ZRANK and ZRANGE. Extra memory: one integer per pointer.

Because it saves memory without slowing searches down: with p = 1/4, nodes have fewer pointers but the expected number of search steps is the same as with p = 1/2.

Pointers per node average 1/(1 − p): 2 for p = 1/2 and 1.33 for p = 1/4, a third less. Redis keeps everything in RAM, so bytes per element matter.

Search steps are about (1/p) · log1/p N. For p = 1/2 that is 2 · log2 N. For p = 1/4 it is 4 · log4 N, and since log4 N is half of log2 N this is also 2 · log2 N.

Example with N = 106: about 40 steps either way, but 10 levels instead of 20. Fewer levels also means fewer pointers to rewrite on each insert. The trade-off is a little more variation in search time from run to run.

code.title: Collinear points: doubles say "turn", scaled integers say "collinear"
code.python:
def cross(ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy):
    return (bx - ax) * (cy - ay) - (by - ay) * (cx - ax)


def main():
    print("Points A(0.1,0.3) B(0.2,0.6) C(0.3,0.9) all lie on the line y = 3x")
    # 1) Plain floats: 0.1, 0.3, 0.9 ... cannot be stored exactly, so the result is a tiny non-zero number.
    d = cross(0.1, 0.3, 0.2, 0.6, 0.3, 0.9)
    print("double, test == 0:       " + ("collinear" if d == 0 else "NOT collinear (wrong)"))
    # 2) Floats with a tolerance: works here, but the tolerance is a guess.
    print("double, test |x| < 1e-9: " + ("collinear" if abs(d) < 1e-9 else "NOT collinear (wrong)"))
    # 3) Scale by 10 and use integers: every step is exact.
    e = cross(1, 3, 2, 6, 3, 9)
    print(f"integers (x10), cross = {e}: " + ("collinear" if e == 0 else "NOT collinear"))
    # The same effect in one line: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in binary floating point.
    print("0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 ? " + ("yes" if 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 else "no")
          + "   1 + 2 == 3 ? " + ("yes" if 1 + 2 == 3 else "no"))
    # Time O(1), space O(1).


main()

followUps:
Because tests with a tolerance can contradict each other, and a hull algorithm that receives contradictory answers can build a shape that cannot exist.

"Nearly collinear" is not consistent the way exact equality is. A, B, C may pass the test and B, C, D may pass it, while A, B, D is clearly a turn. Things that then go wrong:

  • Endless loop: gift wrapping stops when it returns to the start point. If the start was skipped as "collinear", it never returns.
  • Crash: the pop loop in a scan removes more points than expected and reads below the stack; or sorting by angle with an inconsistent comparator fails (Java throws "Comparison method violates its general contract"; C++ sort has undefined behaviour).
  • Wrong hull: a dent is kept or a corner is dropped.

The cure is an exact orientation test, so all answers agree with one real set of points. As a safety net, cap the loop at N steps.

It answers one question: is point D inside, on, or outside the circle through A, B and C? Its main use is building Delaunay triangulations.

A triangulation is Delaunay when no point lies inside the circle around any triangle. The algorithms use the test to decide whether to flip the shared edge of two triangles. From Delaunay you get Voronoi diagrams, good meshes for simulation, nearest-neighbour graphs and terrain models.

Example: A(0,0), B(2,0), C(0,2). Their circle has centre (1,1) and radius2 = 2. D(1,1) is inside, D(2,2) is exactly on it (distance2 = 2), D(3,3) is outside (distance2 = 8).

In code it is the sign of a 3×3 determinant of coordinate differences. It multiplies four coordinates together, so it overflows much sooner than orientation: 64-bit integers are only safe for coordinates up to about 104. Beyond that use 128-bit or big integers, or adaptive exact predicates.

code.title: Union-find with union by size and path compression

followUps:
All three shorten the path during find and give the same O(α(N)) amortized bound; they differ in how many passes they need.

  • Full compression: find the root, then point every node on the path at it. Two passes, or a recursion that can overflow the stack on a long chain.
  • Path halving: one pass; every second node is pointed at its grandparent.
  • Path splitting: one pass; every node is pointed at its grandparent.
while (parent[x] != x) {          // path halving
  parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
  x = parent[x];
}

Example chain 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 (root), calling find(1). Compression: 1, 2, 3, 4 all point to 5. Halving: 1 → 3 and 3 → 5; nodes 2 and 4 are unchanged. Splitting: 1 → 3, 2 → 4, 3 → 5, 4 → 5.

Halving is the usual practical choice: a simple loop, no recursion, no extra memory.

It never deletes anything. It arranges the work so each edge is added exactly while it is alive and then undone, using a segment tree over time.

  1. Read all operations first. Each edge is alive over a time interval, from its insertion to its deletion.
  2. Store that interval in a segment tree over the time line; it lands on O(log Q) nodes.
  3. Walk the tree depth-first. Entering a node, union its edges (by size, no path compression) and push each change on a stack. At a leaf, answer that moment's query. Leaving the node, pop and undo.
// undo one union: c was hung under p
parent[c] = c;
size[p] -= size[c];

Example: edge (1,2) is added at time 0 and removed at time 5. A query at time 3 lies inside its interval and sees 1 and 2 connected; a query at time 7 does not.

Cost: O(E · log Q · log N) time for E edges and Q time steps, O(E log Q) space.
